en: The *Dinakarī* establishes its eternality [with the words] "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*). Regarding the recollection of the means to a desired end conducive to the activity of suckling breast-milk, he says "of a positive entity" (*bhāvasya*) because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) cannot undergo destruction. He says "because destruction is impossible" (*nāśāsambhavāt*).

The meaning is that, since destruction has "being an originated entity" (*janyabhāvatva*) as its cause, and since the self (*ātman*) is beginningless and thus lacks the property of being an originated entity—which is the required cause—destruction is impossible for it.
This concludes the refutation of the Cārvāka view. Now, [the opponent objects]: surely it is only the eyes and other sense organs that [serve as causes] with respect to cognition and so forth?

Let there be both instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*). Instrumentality consists in being a cause while possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*); for in the case of the eye and so forth, when they possess an operation in the form of contact with the eye and so on, they exist at a time immediately preceding the visual cognition. However, it does not consist in being "endowed with the fruit" (*phalopahitatva*).

In such injunctions as "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *rājasūya*," [the definition of agency] would not apply to the instrumentality residing in the sacrifice and so forth, and it would further entail the undesirable consequence that there is no distinction between instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and causality (*kāraṇatva*).
Moreover, although agency cannot consist in possessing an effort (*kṛti*) conducive to an action when applied to an insentient entity, [it must be defined otherwise].

Nevertheless, since the opponent does not accept a distinct self (*ātman*) nor the inherence of actions (*kṛti*) and so forth in such a self, the meaning is that the eyes and other [senses] may themselves be the substrata of action. Now, if one and the same thing were both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), [how could this be?]
Since the distinction between the conventions of agent, instrument, and so forth would otherwise be untenable, he says: "contradiction" (*virodha*).

By "contradiction," he means subsistence in different loci (*vibhinnādhikaraṇavṛttitva*). Thus, the intention is that the distinction between the conventions of agent, instrument, and so forth is established through the difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) characterized by agency, instrumentality, and the like.
And since it is impossible for the word "that" (tat) to refer to the absence that is presented as the substantive in the phrase "not consciousness," he explains: "being such [is] consciousness.
(Dinakari)

Since the term *upaghāta* (impairment) is used exclusively to denote the destruction of a constituent part, he says: "destruction. Regarding the statement in the root text, "How can there be memory when [the mind] is impaired," he says "by implication" (*arthāt*), because there arises an expectation as to whose impairment it is.

Thus, the intention is that the single word "of the senses" (*indriyāṇām*) is connected to both [the preceding and following clauses] by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Regarding the question "How is there memory?"—in the root text, under the view that the senses possess consciousness, the absence of memory is established when the eye is absent; since no reason for this has been stated, [the author] himself provides the reason.

Fulfilling the meaning, he says: "First, by the eye. Now, one might object that memory could arise through another sense organ; therefore, he says: "Of what was experienced by another [organ]. He states the reason for this here:
"Because of experience... [End of Dinakarī]. Although [the two] are in different loci...
Although the statement "by way of co-location" (sāmānādhikaraṇyena) is fruitless because of the absence of a causal relation [between the two], nevertheless,
where there is memory by way of the relation of objectness (viṣayatā), there is experience by way of the relation of objectness;
thus, the causal relation is established through a proximity consisting of co-location defined by such objectness.

It is necessary [to postulate this] because, given a causal relation constituted by the coreferentiality residing in the self (*ātmaniṣṭhasāmānādhikaraṇya*), there would otherwise be no way to prevent the occurrence of a memory regarding a cloth (*paṭa*)— connected to it by the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*)— immediately after the experience of a jar (*ghaṭa*).
This is because the experience produced by the visual organ exists in the jar, yet a memory produced by a different sense organ occurs with respect to that same object.
The statement was made in that way to dispel the doubt that [the objection] is untenable;

its meaning is that the relation of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is constituted by inherence (*samavāya*). When the qualification "belonging to that person" (*tatpuruṣīyatva*) is introduced in order to prevent Maitra from remembering a jar at the time Caitra is experiencing a jar, [the following occurs].

The intended meaning is that it should be understood as follows: because it would be cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate an infinite causal relationship between the two due to the difference in individuals,
one accepts their status as cause and effect through the proximity (pratyāsatti) of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as mediated by inherence (samavāya).

Thus ends the refutation of the view of those who maintain that the senses [are conscious]. To indicate that the defect which exists in the position that the senses possess consciousness does not apply to this present theory, he says: "of the eternal," etc.

Dinakarī: Now, in the root text, the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "not so" (*na tathā*) would refer only to consciousness (*caitanya*) as previously presented; thus, there would be an inconsistency. Therefore, he says: "not so, not consciousness."

"It would then be without a supervisor" (*anadhyakṣam*); by this, it is stated that cognition and so forth are not perceived when the mind is itself conscious, as expressed by the root [verse]. Demonstrating the reason for that, he says: "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*).

"The perception of that" (*tatpratyakṣa*) means the impossibility of the perception of cognition and so forth. But [an objection]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "nanu". The translation reflects the available portion.]

The minute size of the mind (*manas*) is itself unestablished; therefore, he says, "And just as... [and] "will be explained later. The meaning is that this will be proven by the passage: "Because cognitions are not simultaneous, its minuteness is accepted here. [Regarding the phrase] "consciousness alone": this refers to the definition of the self (*ātman*).

It should be understood that it is called "self" (ātman) because it is the subject under discussion, since in his view even the mere entity (*vastumātra*) has the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Here, there is a dispute as to whether the state of being consciousness (*vijñānatva*) is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) or of existence (*sattva*); in this regard, the affirmative position (*vidhikoṭi*) belongs to the Yogācāra.
It should be understood that the negative position belongs to the Naiyāyika. Consciousness is twofold:

the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Among these, "this is a jar" and so forth constitute the evolving consciousness; [the other] is the storehouse consciousness. Among these, this...
The active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) such as "this is a jar," and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) such as "I know"—
that alone is the self (*ātman*). [This is from] Dinakari, verse 2.1.2.

[Regarding] consciousness: [an objection is raised] that the self would not be established in deep sleep, because the previously arisen consciousness has perished due to its momentariness, and there is no cause for the arising of another consciousness at that time; therefore, he says:
"the preceding, preceding... [He continues: "But [is it not the case that] because of the momentariness of consciousness..."

He dispels the objection that, because the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) dependent upon that [cognition] is also momentary, there could be no recollection at a later time— by means of the words "mṛgamada" and so forth. Having raised the alternative as to whether the intended object-sphere of consciousness is the entire world or some particular object, he addresses the first case:
He states the refutation with the words "of that" (*tasya*). [This refers to] consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the second [alternative], he says "whatever" (*yatkiṃcit*).
He states the refutation of the view that the consciousness of the self's own nature has an object with the words "in deep sleep" (*suṣuptau*).

He raises an objection with the words "at that time" (*tadānīm*). [The consciousness] is formless and objectless; it is a continuum of consciousness (*citsantati*), that is, a continuum of cognition (*vijñānasantati*).
"In luminosity" means "in being cognition. The sense is that the property of being cognition (jñānatva) is pervaded by objectivity (viṣayitā).

"Otherwise" means even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), if one were to accept the status of being cognition therein. Having raised the dilemma as to whether the form (ākāra) is distinct from consciousness or not distinct, he states the refutation regarding the first alternative: "Then..."

Regarding the phrase "has arrived": he says [in response] to the second [objection], "as a collective apprehension" (*samūhālambana*). The meaning is that "blue and yellow" refers to a collective apprehension. He says "it would be so," the sense being that there is a rule that what is non-different from that which is non-different from something else must itself be non-different from that thing. He establishes this very point—starting with "by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*)—as follows:
"Of consciousness" means "of the nature of consciousness. This is because there is no distinction, that is, because it is one.

Now, one might object: the blue form and the yellow form are indeed non-different; the perception of difference arises only from the difference between their two attributes, namely blueness and yellowness. And yet, even those two...

Intending to show that there can be no identity because the nature of consciousness is distinct from non-ultimate qualities such as blueness—since identity between the ultimate consciousness and what is non-ultimate is impossible—the author raises an objection with the words "in the form of an exclusion" (*apoharūpa*).
This means "in the form of the exclusion of the non-blue. Otherwise...

Regarding the coexistence of contradictory qualities such as blueness and so forth in a single locus: [the opponent might argue] that in a cognition apprehending a collection (*samūhālambana*), neither the form of blue nor the form of yellow is admitted; rather, it is only a variegated form (*citrākāra*) that is accepted, and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he primarily refutes the theory of the transfer of latent impressions (*vāsanāsaṃkrama*) with the words "nor... (*na vā*).

Regarding the phrase "of the mother and the son": the sense is that there would be the undesirable consequence of a memory in the child residing in the womb of what was experienced by the mother. He also refutes the view that "what is experienced by the material cause (upādāna) is remembered by its effect (upādeya)" with the words "nor... He raises an objection with the words "in the subsequent [moment]...": the meaning of "its producer" (tadutpādaka) is "the producer of the latent impression" (vāsanā).

"Citām eva" means that if only cognitions were to produce impressions (*saṃskāra*), then because those cognitions are infinite, it would follow that the impressions are also infinite. He raises an objection: "Kṣaṇika...
[etc. An "excellent quality" (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*) is a specific power (*śakti-viśeṣa*). [This occurs] by way of being associated with each subsequent cognition.

The remainder [of the commentary] follows. Regarding the phrase "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*): the meaning is that it is simpler to accept the identity of this very object through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) held even by common folk—namely, "this is that very same thing"—rather than to postulate an infinite number of momentary potencies (*śakti*), their prior absences (*prāgabhāva*), and their subsequent destructions (*dhvaṃsa*). Now, one might object: "An sprout does not arise from a seed situated in a field..."

It is accepted that the seed situated in the granary is the cause of that which is delimited by sprout-ness (*aṅkuratvāvacchinna*) by virtue of its being of a "productive nature" (*kurvadrūpatva*). And this "productive nature" is a specific universal (*jāti*) established as the delimitor of the causal capacity for producing a sprout; and that [universal]...
Just as [in the case of seeds], a state of being a seed is postulated as being pervaded by the mere capacity of a momentary, efficient seed to produce its fruit,

so too here, it must be stated that the production of latencies (vāsanā) residing in successive bodies within momentary bodies occurs precisely through the nature of being "kuru-drūpa" (performing its function). Therefore...

He says: "In the case of seeds and so forth. This refers to the logical justification for the restriction that a sprout arises from a certain seed and not from another; [this is justified] because one does not postulate the state of being a "producing entity" (*kurvadrūpa*) in seeds and such things situated in a granary.

The point is that since the sprout cannot arise simply due to the absence of auxiliary causes such as contact with soil and water, one need not postulate a "productive nature" (*kurvadrūpatva*) nor a causal efficiency in that form, as there is no evidence for it.
On this point, they say: by the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever exists is momentary," [the momentariness] of the entire world...

Momentariness, and in accordance with that, the state of being "productive" (*kurvadrūpatva*)—that is, being a cause toward an effect by virtue of such a form—is necessary. Nor is there a lack of evidence for such a pervasion (*vyāpti*);
for if such a pervasion were not accepted, one would have to prevent the production of a sprout from a seed situated in a granary [by postulating a causal capacity].
If one were to postulate that the contact between the earth and water and other factors acts as auxiliary causes (sahakārin), it would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

However, by accepting such a pervasion (vyāpti), one can instead postulate "productive nature" (kurvadrūpatva) as the cause; thus, since the seed remaining in the granary lacks this productive nature, the non-arising of the sprout is naturally accounted for.

The state of being a co-operating cause (*sahakāritā*) belongs to the other causal factors; this is due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, even in the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that it is specifically the seed, or the conjunction of the earth and water, that possesses the "producing form" (*kurvadrūpa*) and thus constitutes the cause; therefore, it is necessary to postulate that all these co-operating factors possess causal status.

This must be stated: in my view, seeds and their auxiliaries—such as the contact with earth and water—are postulated as causes toward the sprout solely by virtue of being *kurvadrūpa* (that which is performing the action); however, if *kurvadrūpatva* is not admitted...

This is because it would be cumbersome to postulate various causal factors, such as being a seed, being in contact with the soil, and so forth. Nor should it be argued that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), since those [factors] are established as having a single cause by virtue of possessing "productive form" (*kurvadrūpa*), such cumbersomeness is not a fault because it is "aimed at the result" (*phalamukha*); for even cumbersomeness aimed at the result [is a fault].

Because it is a fault. Furthermore, if the world were momentary, recognition in the form "this is that very same jar" would be untenable, because the non-difference from the jar of the previous time would not exist in the jar of the present time.
Nor can it be argued that the object of such a cognition is merely non-difference of the *jāti* (universal), for in that [momentarist] view, even the *jāti* is momentary.

Because, due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), the pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) residing in a pot at a previous time does not exist in a pot at this [present] time. By this, the following [argument] is also refuted: "If the world were momentary, there would be only a single causal relation for that which is delimited by destruction (*nāśatva*); thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, as for what was said...

If one accepts that entities are stable, then since capacity and incapacity are contradictory within a single entity, it follows that they must be distinct; however, that too is not correct. For it is only within a single entity, at the delimitation of a single time, that capacity and its absence are contradictory, whereas [they are not contradictory] across different times.

Because there is no subverting evidence against accepting that [distinction]. As for the objection that, if the substrata existing at earlier and later times were non-different, then the distinction between their properties—efficacy and inefficacy—would be untenable because, in that view, property and substratum are non-different:
that is not so. For pot-ness is not the pot.

Since it is impossible to assert the non-difference of the attribute and the substratum due to the resulting invalidity of such cognitions as those mentioned above, this is the general direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of the proponents of momentariness.
The Vedāntin raises an objection: "Let it be so, then. Regarding the phrase "momentary consciousness":

this means the position that the self has the nature of momentary consciousness. Having raised the alternative—that the mere self possesses the nature of eternal consciousness like that of God—he states the refutation of the first [position] with the words "of that" (*tasya*).

"Because it has been shown" means that this has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "its having the world as its object," and so forth. Thus, the sense is that since it is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to possess such a nature, the self in its entirety cannot have the nature of eternal knowledge. [Objection: But surely the individual soul does not have the world as its object.

We do not claim that [the self] has as its object everything whatsoever that is new; rather, we say that it has as its object whatever object is established by experience in a particular living being. Therefore, he says: "of having an object. Now, one might object:
the scripture itself, "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyaṃ jñānam*), is the very authority for the fact that the living being is of the nature of knowledge. Thus...

He says: "True. Now, since the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman are one, it follows without obstruction that the soul is of the nature of eternal consciousness; therefore, he establishes the difference between the soul and Brahman with the words: "knowledge and ignorance," etc. By the phrase "happiness and so forth," suffering is included. [The word] "sutarām" means "all the more."

The sense is that once the plurality of individual souls (jīvātman) is established, it is impossible for the one Lord (īśvara) to consist of multiple individual souls, because unity and plurality are contradictory.

The meaning is that the distinction between the Lord and the individual soul (īśvarajīvātman-bheda) is thereby established; otherwise, if the Lord were identical with the individual soul, [there would be no distinction]. [This leads to the problem of] bondage and liberation.

The meaning is that the distinction—that some transmigrating being is bound and another is liberated—would be untenable; the intention is that this is because the selves of Caitra and Maitra are one with the nature of the Lord.
[Objection: But how then [is it explained] regarding Brahman, which is denoted by the word "That" in such passages as "That thou art"?

He says "Even that which... because the Veda, which conveys the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the word *yuṣmad* [from Brahman], is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He refutes the view that non-difference with Brahman arises for individual souls at the time of liberation—by stating "mokṣa" [and so on]. This is done even while accepting that difference is impermanent.

At the time of liberation, he establishes the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman with the words "even when the difference has perished. By the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that as long as the difference exists, the two individuals are beyond dispute; this refers to you, the Vedāntins. The phrase "devoid of attributes" (*nirdharmaka*) is used here [to mean] even in the absence of reality (*satyatva*).

It has been stated as the cause. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmakatva*)—meaning being empty of attributes distinct from itself—is not untenable? This is because truth (*satyatva*), which consists in the absence of falsity (*mithyātva*), is of the nature of Brahman, and because an absence (*abhāva*) is identical with its locus (*adhikaraṇātma*). It is with this intention that [the author] says:

He raises an objection: "the absence of falsity. Now, one might ask: how can there be duality, which is the absence of oneness, in a locus of oneness? To this he says: "each individually. Now, what is the status of the scriptural passage, "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman," which implies that non-difference arises at the time of liberation? To this he says: "even that which... For this very reason, [he cites] the scripture: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman."
Precisely because it establishes equality. *Dinakarī*: "Virañjana" means free from suffering.

Regarding the second [point], he states the defect: "Even Īśvara... By the word "vijñāna," he refers to the word "vijñāna" occurring within such scriptural passages (*śrutyanta*) as "eternal" (*nitya*), etc., using the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is: "because it makes known [Brahman] as the substratum of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "as having bliss" (*ānandavat*): the intention is that by means of the word *ānanda* ending in the possessive suffix *-vat*, one understands [Brahman] as possessing bliss;
otherwise, the neuter form *ānandam* would be untenable. Now, [an objection]: the meaning "as having bliss" is not consistent with your own position regarding the Lord (*īśvara*).
Because there is an absence of bliss [in that case], he says: "Bliss also... Since the very assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is your fault, he says:

"Or let it be... Regarding the phrase "not happiness" (*asukham*): the sense is that, according to the Neo-Logicians (*navya*), this indicates a difference between Brahman and happiness. [He mentions] "because of the occurrence of an undesirable assumption."

The meaning is that, in order to obtain the sense of another word (anyapadārtha) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a new figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be applied there; otherwise, [if it were not so], a figurative indication would necessarily apply even in a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound. It should not be argued that a figurative indication for the negative particle (*nañ*) is unavoidable because, otherwise, the meaning of the negative particle could not be construed through difference since it would then be the meaning of a noun (*nāma*). For, even though it is a noun...

"Because it is a particle (*nipāta*). [Objection: But even in a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—characterized by the two words 'asukha' and 'brahma' denoting a single substratum—is established by experience; otherwise, their agreement in case-number (*samānavacanatva*) would be inexplicable. Therefore, for the sake of accounting for that [coreferentiality]...

Since even for you, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that which possesses the absence of [the primary meaning] is necessary, he says: "Because of the context," etc. And because of the contradiction with the suffix: the meaning is that the form *ānandam* cannot be accounted for without a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-ac*) due to the rule that the word *ānanda* is invariably masculine. Thus it ends.

The refutation of the Vedānta view. He sets forth the Sāṃkhya view in order to refute it, with the words "by this" (etena). This means by the previously stated reasoning that establishes the Self as possessing knowledge, and by the reasoning to be stated hereafter. [He says] "primordial nature" (prakṛti).

The meaning is "the primal nature" (mūlaprakṛti). Regarding the term "agent" (kartrī): agency here consists in being the material cause of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which acts as the agent. It should be noted that, according to that school's view, agency characterized by the possession of an inclination toward action is a property of the internal organ. "Like a lotus leaf" means like a lotus petal. And just as...

The meaning is that just as a lotus leaf smeared with water does not become wet, so too the Puruṣa does not undergo the attribution of agency and the like. Thus, the inference—"the Puruṣa possesses the absence of agency because it lacks causality"—should be understood as the proof in this regard. Now, [one might object] there...

Because [the reason] would lack a causal basis, the probans (*hetu*) is unestablished; therefore, he says: "of the effect and the cause. "It would not exist" means "let it not be. "Of that person" refers to the Puruṣa. Now, what is the proof for the existence of such a person?
To this he says: "residing in the intellect" (*buddhigata*). It is precisely consciousness (*caitanya*), which is well-known in some instances...

The meaning is that [the attribution of agency] is possible because it is superimposed upon the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "from primordial nature" (prakṛteḥ), the sense is "from the root-primal nature. Now, if the person lacks agency, then since dharma and adharma cannot arise therein, and consequently pleasure and pain dependent upon them do not arise therein—
Liberation, which consists in the destruction of suffering, would not belong to the *puruṣa*;
therefore, he says: "by the existence or non-existence of that. This means by the existence or non-existence of the *buddhi-sattva*.
When the *buddhi-sattva* exists, through the channel of the senses and by its transformation, this [consciousness] perceives the jar.

An object such as a jar, connected with a cognition such as "this," resides in the *puruṣa* (the self) by way of a relation consisting in the non-apprehension of a non-relation [between itself] and the intellect (*buddhi*), which undergoes transformation into the form of its own cognition. (Dinakarī)

By concealing the true nature of the *puruṣa*, [the intellect] brings about the transmigratory existence of the *puruṣa*; however, upon the destruction of the intellect, because its transformations— such as the cognition "this is a jar"— cease to exist, there is an absence of delimitation by objects, resulting in the state of abiding in isolation (*kaivalya*).

Liberation consists in the cessation of that bad connection; the meaning is that both transmigratory existence and liberation belong not to the Spirit (puruṣa), but rather to the intellect (buddhi) alone. Now, one might object: let there be a direct connection with objects in the Spirit itself, and let that very [connection] be the regulator of the empirical usage of transmigratory existence for it.
To the question, "By what kind of relationship—is it a relationship through a series constructed by the intellect?"—he says: "Of that very [intellect].

Thus, the relationship of the self with the object is actually the relationship of the intellect; this is because there is a non-apprehension of the non-connection between the intellect and the self, and not because of any independence on the part of the self.

There is no connection with the object, because there is a lack of evidence. Nor should it be argued that, for the sake of illuminating the object, a direct connection must be accepted rather than the aforementioned indirect succession;
for if that [connection] were dependent on the nature of the Puruṣa, then since the Puruṣa is eternal...
Because there would follow the consequence of the impossibility of liberation, since the connection with an object depends upon its own nature;

for at the time when a jar is manifested, since there exists a connection between consciousness and the form of the cloth or other objects— which depends upon the nature of those objects such as the cloth— the manifestation of the cloth and so forth would also necessarily occur.

He states the distinction between *buddhi* (intellect) and *jñāna* (knowledge) with the words "of that very [intellect]"; thus, the sense is that knowledge is a transformation (*pariṇati*) of the intellect, and not the intellect itself. Regarding the phrase "due to the non-apprehension of difference":

the meaning is "due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the intellect and the *puruṣa*. Now, for the purpose of showing the distinction between apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and the intellect:

Dinakari: He demonstrates the three components of cognition with the words "This is mine," and so forth. Just as the connection of a mirror with a face is merely a reflection and not real, so too is the "coloration" (uparāga) of the Puruṣa—that is, its relation to the Puruṣa.

The meaning is that the "coloration" (uparāga) of the puruṣa is the conceit of identity arising from the non-apprehension of the difference between the intellect (buddhi) and the puruṣa. Through the channel of the senses— that is, by way of the senses— there occurs a specific transformation (pariṇāmabheda) of the intellect in the form of cognitions such as "this is a jar," which [occurs] with respect to an object such as a jar.
The meaning is "connection. Regarding its ultimate reality, the example is the tarnish on a mirror struck by one's own breath. As for the phrase "that 'this must be done'":

the manifestation of objects such as pots that are to be made arises through the aforementioned two types of superimposition—namely, the superimposition upon the Person (puruṣa) and the superimposition upon the object.

The meaning is that the "aspect of activity" (*vyāpārāṃśa*) is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this must be done. Regarding the statement "the non-real connection of the person with cognition," the grammatical construction here is: that non-real connection which exists between the person and cognition is called "perception" (*upalabdhi*).
The example is unreal, like the connection of the face with the dirt on the mirror. Thus,

the unreal connection of the conscious "I" with the cognition— having the form "I know this"— which is superimposed upon the intellect (buddhi), is what constitutes perception (upalabdhi), and not [the connection with external objects].

The meaning of Dinakari’s statement "cognition itself is apprehension" is as follows: regarding the phrase "by way of coreferentiality with volition," although the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) is supersensible, it should be understood that in the aspect [of the cognition] "I, who am righteous, am acting," there is a cognition in the form of a presented object (upanītabhāna). This is because [the unseen merit] is subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva).

The meaning is: "because it is the substratum for impermanent phenomena. Regarding the phrase "of action, unseen potential (adṛṣṭa), and experience": action produces an unseen potential that has the very same locus as itself, and that unseen potential produces an experience that has the very same locus as itself; thus [it is the substratum] of action, unseen potential, and experience.

The meaning is that, just as there is a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through a traditional succession [of teachers], so too there is the experience of a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality in the form "I, who am conscious, act.

Regarding the phrase "distinct from that" (*tadbhinna*), it means distinct from the agent. The word "ca" (and) connects with the phrase "due to the absence of proof," which refers to the [proposition] beginning with "conscious" (*cetana*).

This [particle] "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the previously mentioned objections. One might object: "If the locus of agency is not the conscious self, because it is the locus of produced attributes like a jar—since such a subverting argument exists, the cognition 'I, who am consciousness, act' must be an error regarding the aspect of consciousness. To this, he replies: "[It is not so], even regarding the aspect of action."
The intellect (*buddhi*) is devoid of agency because it is the locus of produced attributes; thus, the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) applies there as well.

The meaning is "because of existence. "Otherwise" means: if one accepts a distinction between the agent and consciousness. Regarding "the eternity of consciousness": if one accepts a conscious principle distinct from the agent, then because there would be an absence of pleasure and pain in that [conscious principle], transmigration and liberation would be untenable according to the manner previously stated.
Transmigration and liberation must be explained solely through the existence and non-existence of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Thus, if the intellect were eternal, transmigration—which is contingent upon its existence—would occur at all times, resulting in the impossibility of liberation. Conversely, if the intellect were non-eternal, it must be admitted that it is produced, for that which is unproduced [cannot cease].
Because its destruction is impossible. Thus, the meaning is that prior to its production, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—which is dependent upon its existence—would not occur.

In reality, because of the absence of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors residing in it prior to its production, transmigratory existence would never arise due to the non-arising of the intellect (*buddhi*).

This should be noted. Regarding the phrase "because of non-establishment" (asiddheḥ): the sense is that [the intellect] lacks the status of being an effect of primordial matter (prakṛti) within the cognition [of its own nature].

Now, one might object: "By means of the inference of being produced based on its being an agent, and through the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), the cognition would have the production by primordial matter as its object. To this, he says: "Of the agent" (kartuḥ).
The point is that if agency were pervaded by being produced (*janyatva*), there would be no supporting reasoning (*anukūlatarka*).

On the contrary, since there exists reasoning that establishes the opposite—namely, beginninglessness—he states that the agent is indeed beginningless: "vītarāga... [referring to] the *Nyāyasūtra*: "Because the birth of one free from passion is not observed."
The meaning of that is: "because one observes births accompanied by passion. Regarding "beginninglessness": in the case of drinking breast milk...
